candidate_sources.title: Blue and Green Mold of Citrus / Home and Landscape / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: UC IPM Pest Management Guideline for blue and green mold of citrus caused by Penicillium italicum (blue mold) and Penicillium digitatum (green mold). Describes symptoms (soft, watery, odorous decay with white mycelium and blue or green spores), infection through wounds, and management including sanitation, careful handling, and cool storage.

candidate_sources.title: Penicillium italicum: An Underexplored Postharvest Pathogen
candidate_sources.snippet: Penicillium italicum Wehmer is the causing agent of the blue mold disease of citrus. The pathogen infects fruits through wounds, causing water-soaked areas, white mycelium, and abundant sporulation producing greenish-blue spores. Reviews biology, epidemiology, and current and emerging management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Alternative Management Approaches of Citrus Diseases Caused by Penicillium digitatum (Green Mold) and Penicillium italicum (Blue Mold)
candidate_sources.snippet: Review of postharvest blue mold (Penicillium italicum) and green mold (Penicillium digitatum) of citrus. Covers symptoms, short disease cycle (3-5 days at 25 C), resistance to common fungicides (imazalil, pyrimethanil, fludioxonil, thiabendazole), and alternative control using antagonistic microorganisms, essential oils, chitosan coatings, heat treatments, and food additives.

candidate_sources.title: HS995/HS241: Field Identification of Citrus Blight
candidate_sources.snippet: An easy and rapid field test for blight is to inject water with a syringe into the trunk of the tree. Trees that have blight will not accept water via the syringe test method regardless of the amount of pressure applied. First symptoms on HLB-free trees are usually a mild wilting and grayish cast to the foliage, often accompanied by zinc deficiency symptoms.

candidate_sources.title: PP-180/CG038: 2025–2026 Florida Citrus Production Guide: Blight
candidate_sources.snippet: Citrus blight is a wilt-and-decline disease of citrus, and its cause has not been determined. Trees affected by blight grow normally until they reach five to six years of age or older and then begin to wilt and to exhibit leaf loss, reduced growth flushes, die back and general decline. The causal agent for blight remains undetermined.

candidate_sources.title: Citrus blight disease (citrus blight) - Plantwise Plus Knowledge Bank (CABI)
candidate_sources.snippet: Citrus blight disease datasheet covering the distribution, symptoms, host range, and management of the disease affecting citrus trees including sweet orange. The rootstocks most severely affected are rough lemon, Rangpur lime, trifoliate orange, and Carrizo citrange; most tolerant are sweet orange, sour orange, and Cleopatra mandarin.

candidate_sources.title: Penicillium digitatum (green mould) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on Penicillium digitatum, the causal agent of green mould of citrus — covers pathogen identity, distribution, hosts, symptoms, biology, epidemiology, and management of postharvest green mold on oranges and other citrus.

candidate_sources.title: Pre- and Postharvest Treatments to Control Green Mold of Citrus Fruit During Ethylene Degreening | Plant Disease (APS)
candidate_sources.snippet: Plant Disease (APS) article on pre- and postharvest treatments to control green mold (Penicillium digitatum) of citrus fruit during ethylene degreening — discussing fungicides such as imazalil, thiabendazole, and integrated approaches to reduce green mold decay in oranges.

candidate_sources.title: Citrus Greening (Huanglongbing) - Citrus Research and Education Center (CREC) - University of Florida, IFAS
candidate_sources.snippet: Citrus greening (Huanglongbing, HLB) is one of the most destructive diseases of citrus worldwide. Caused by the phloem-limited bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus and vectored by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri). Symptoms include blotchy mottle of leaves, lopsided/misshapen fruit with color inversion, twig dieback, and tree decline.

candidate_sources.title: Huanglongbing of Citrus - University of Arizona Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet on Huanglongbing (HLB) of citrus describing the causal agent (Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus), the Asian citrus psyllid vector, characteristic blotchy yellow asymmetrical leaf mottling, lopsided bitter fruit, twig dieback, and management recommendations including vector control and use of disease-free planting material.

candidate_sources.title: Citrus Huanglongbing (Greening) Disease | Plant Health Cases (CABI)
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Plant Health Case study on citrus Huanglongbing (HLB), the most damaging disease of citrus worldwide. Caused by three closely related Candidatus Liberibacter species (asiaticus, africanus, americanus); spread by psyllid vectors and infected planting material; confirmed in over 60 countries. Covers symptoms, diagnosis, epidemiology, and management.

candidate_sources.title: CIR359A/CH081: 2025-2026 Florida Citrus Production Guide: Decay Control of Florida Fresh Citrus
candidate_sources.snippet: UF/IFAS publication covering the most common postharvest fungal decays of Florida citrus including green mold (Penicillium digitatum) and blue mold (Penicillium italicum), with decay control recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Blue and Green Mold of Citrus / Home and Landscape / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: Blue and green mold cause an odorous, soft, watery decay that makes citrus fruit inedible. Green mold is caused by Penicillium digitatum and blue mold is caused by Penicillium italicum, and both result in substantial economic losses around the globe.

candidate_sources.title: Citrus storage moulds (197) - Lucid Apps / Pacific Pests, Pathogens & Weeds
candidate_sources.snippet: Citrus storage moulds caused by Penicillium digitatum (green mould) and Penicillium italicum (blue mould). Symptoms, host range, signs/diagnosis and management of these postharvest pathogens of orange and other citrus fruit.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Penicillium ulaiense Causing Postharvest Whisker Mold of Oranges (Citrus sinensis) in Spain
candidate_sources.snippet: Whisker mold, caused by Penicillium ulaiense, is a postharvest disease of oranges (Citrus sinensis). Symptoms include water-soaked circular lesions with a blue-gray spore mass and distinctive whisker-like coremia (1–8 mm) with white stalks, distinguishing it from blue mold caused by P. italicum.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Whisker Mold of Citrus (Citrus sinensis) Caused by Penicillium ulaiense in Pakistan
candidate_sources.snippet: Whisker mold caused by Penicillium ulaiense is a postharvest disease of sweet orange (Citrus sinensis). The pathogen produces grayish-blue conidial masses on soft lesions with whisker-like coremia bearing tall whitish stalks, and was confirmed by morphological characters and molecular analysis.

candidate_sources.title: First report of whisker mold, a postharvest disease on citrus caused by Penicillium ulaiense (in Japan)
candidate_sources.snippet: Whisker mold symptoms include water-soaked circular lesions with a blue-gray spore mass and coremia with white stalks and mycelia in the outer periphery of the lesion. The causal fungus was identified as Penicillium ulaiense based on morphological characteristics and β-tubulin gene phylogenetic analysis. Disease symptoms appeared on inoculated fruit after 7 days at 25°C, fulfilling Koch's postulates.
